newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa seeks rating reward for economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa seeks rating reward for economic reforms.

text.p: South Africa, its long-term debt sitting on the cusp of investment grade, could be rewarded for recent economic reforms with a crucial rating upgrade later this year, analysts and economists said on Tuesday.

Moody's Investor's Services already rates the country an investment prospect at Baa3. But Standard and Poor's has its long-term foreign currency debt pegged one notch below at BB+, though with a positive outlook.
Guido Cipriani, S&P director responsible for South Africa, said that prospects had improved since the agency's last visit in September 1996.

"I think the developments since our last visit have been quite encouraging. There are no major areas where we are seriously concerned that things have not met expectations," he told Reuters by telephone from New York.

"But there are fundamental issues which need to be dealt with which are intrinsically difficult and will take time. So one should be careful about assuming that some progress is necessarily going to lead to a change in credit rating."
Cipriani said areas where the government needed to prove itself included sustained fiscal discipline, more privatisation, exchange control liberalisation and labour market reform.
He declined to comment on when S&P would next review its rating. However, finance ministry sources said they expected the agency to return around September this year.

Economists said an investment rating from S&P, backing up the existing Moody's view, would open up South African debt to a wider band of investors, including many U.S. funds which are barred from buying speculative grade debt.
The move would also increase the ability of government and other South African institutions to raise funds offshore, and cut their borrowing costs.

Magan Mistry of Nedcor bank said steps to ease exchange controls in the March budget were encouraging for an upgrade, as was the successful conclusion of the first major privatisation deal in the sale of 30 percent of telecommunications utility Telkom.
Coupled with steady progress in bringing down the budget deficit to a targeted four percent of GDP in 1997/98, the outlook was positive for an upgrade, he said.
"I think there is a fair chance that S&P will upgrade to investment grade, but it won't be more than one notch (to BBB-)," he said.
Jac Laubscher, chief economist at life assurance company Sanlam, agreed: "We are cautiously optimistic that we may get an improvement in the rating to investment grade by one notch."

Other analysts said S&P and rival rating agencies, including IBCA which is expected to review its BB rating later this year, would be taking a hard look at how the country managed the lifting of capital controls on individuals in July.

Anastasia Gekis of ABN Amro in Johannesburg said an upgrade could be on the cards towards the year end, assuming rand markets maintain their new-found stability and the central bank succeeded in reining in money supply and credit growth.

But any upgrade was seen as unlikely before the launch of the government's next international bonds. The Department of Finance last month mandated Merrill Lynch to lead manage a Yankee issue while Daiwa will lead a planned Samurai.
One London-based analyst said South Africa's long-term rating was finely balanced, but saw low foreign reserves as its Achilles heel.
"It's clear that South Africa is a borderline case -- that's why the Moody's model just shifts it into investment grade while S&P still has it speculative," he said.
"The problem is they still have very, very low foreign exchange reserves. The risk is that if something happens, the reserves are simply not there to cover the situation."
Official foreign exchange and gold reserves have risen steadily this year and will get a further boost from this month's inflow of $1.26 billion from the Telkom sale.
But at 14.4 billion rand in April, they equate to only around six weeks import cover. That compares with investment grade emerging markets like Hungary and Poland with five months cover.
